1.1.html:
Definition 1.1. A set-universe is a set \(\mathcal U\) whose elements are sets satisfying the following properties:

  • (Infinite) the set of natural number \(\mathbb N\in\mathcal U\).
  • (Subset closure) if \(A\in\mathcal U\) and \(B\subseteq A\), then \(B\in\mathcal U\);
  • (Power set closure) if \(A\in\mathcal U\), then its power set \(\mathcal P(A)\in\mathcal U\);
  • (Union closure) if \(I\in\mathcal U\) and \(A_i\in\mathcal U\), for each \(i\in I\), then \(\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i\in\mathcal U\).

1.2.html:
Remark 1.2. A similar proof to Russell’s paradox applies here to show that \(\mathcal U\notin\mathcal U\). By contradiction, suppose that \(\mathcal U\in\mathcal U\). Then we can form the subset of \(\mathcal U\)

$$R:=\{A\in\mathcal U\mid A\notin A\}\subseteq\mathcal U$$

and, by hypothesis, we have that \(R\in\mathcal U\). But this gives a contradiction since we have that \(R\in R\) if and only if \(R\notin R\).

1.3.html:
Convention 1.3. We will assume that there exist set-universes

$$\mathcal U_{\mathrm{small}}\subseteq\mathcal U_{\mathrm{large}}\subseteq\mathcal U_{\mathrm{huge}}$$

such that \(\mathcal U_{\mathrm{small}}\in\mathcal U_{\mathrm{large}}\) and \(\mathcal U_{\mathrm{large}}\in\mathcal U_{\mathrm{huge}}\).

1.4.html:
Definition 1.4. We introduce the following terminology.

  • A set or a small set is an element of \(\mathcal U_{\mathrm{small}}\).
  • A large set is an element of \(\mathcal U_{\mathrm{large}}\).
  • A huge set is an element of \(\mathcal U_{\mathrm{huge}}\).

1.5.html:
Definition 1.5. A strict category \(\mathcal C\) consists of

  • a large set \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)\) of objects \(x,y,z,\ldots\);
  • for all objects \(x,y\in\mathcal C\), a large set \(\mathcal C(x,y)\) of morphisms \(f:x\to y\) from \(x\) to \(y\);
  • for each object \(x\in\mathcal C\), an identity morphism \(\operatorname{id}_x:x\to x\);
  • for all morphisms \(f:x\to y\) and \(g:y\to z\) in \(\mathcal C\), a composite morphism \(g\circ f:x\to z\); we also write simply \(gf\) for the composite;

satisfying the following axioms:

  • composition is unital: for each morphism \(f:x\to y\),

$$f\circ\operatorname{id}_x=f\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{id}_y\circ f=f;$$

  • composition is associative: for all morphisms \(f:x\to y\), \(g:y\to z\), and \(h:z\to t\) in \(\mathcal C\),

$$(h\circ g)\circ f=h\circ(g\circ f).$$

1.6.html:
Remark 1.6. By convention, a strict category has a large set of objects, which we refer to simply as its object set, and large sets of morphisms, which we refer to simply as its hom sets.

We will also consider huge strict categories with huge sets of objects and of morphisms.

1.7.html:
Definition 1.7. A strict category \(\mathcal C\) is

  • locally small if, for all objects \(x,y\in\mathcal C\), the hom set \(\mathcal C(x,y)\) is small;
  • small if its object set is small and it is locally small.

1.8.html:
Example 1.8. We have the following examples of strict categories.

  • The strict category \(\mathcal{Set}\) of sets and functions.
  • The strict category \(\mathcal{Set}_{\bullet}\) of pointed sets and basepoint-preserving functions.
  • For a field \(k\), the strict category \(\mathcal{Vect}_k\) of \(k\)-vector spaces and \(k\)-linear maps.
  • The strict category \(\mathcal{Top}\) of topological spaces and continuous functions.

All these strict categories are locally small, but not small.

1.9.html:
Definition 1.9. Let \(\mathcal C\) be a strict category. A morphism \(f:x\to y\) in \(\mathcal C\) is an isomorphism if there is a morphism \(g:y\to x\) in \(\mathcal C\) such that \(g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_x\) and \(f\circ g=\operatorname{id}_y\). We write \(f:x\overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow}y\) or \(f:x\cong y\). We call \(g\) an inverse of \(f\).

We say that two objects \(x\) and \(y\) in \(\mathcal C\) are isomorphic if there is an isomorphism \(f:x\overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow}y\) in \(\mathcal C\). We write \(x\cong y\).

1.10.html:
Example 1.10. The strict categories in Example 1.8 have the following isomorphisms.

  • An isomorphism in \(\mathcal{Set}\) is a bijection.
  • An isomorphism in \(\mathcal{Set}_{\bullet}\) is a basepoint-preserving bijection.
  • An isomorphism in \(\mathcal{Vect}_k\) is a linear bijection.
  • An isomorphism in \(\mathcal{Top}\) is a homeomorphism.

1.11.html:
Proposition 1.11. Let \(\mathcal C\) be a strict category. An isomorphism \(f:x\to y\) in \(\mathcal C\) has a unique inverse, which we denote by \(f^{-1}:y\to x\).

Proof. Suppose that \(g,h:y\to x\) are two inverses of \(f\) in \(\mathcal C\). Then

$$g=g\circ\operatorname{id}_y=g\circ(f\circ h)=(g\circ f)\circ h=\operatorname{id}_x\circ h=h.\quad\square$$

1.12.html:
Definition 1.12. Given strict categories \(\mathcal C\) and \(\mathcal D\), a functor \(F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) consists of:

  • a function \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)\to\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal D)\) sending an object \(x\in\mathcal C\) to an object \(Fx\in\mathcal D\);
  • for all objects \(x,y\in\mathcal C\), a function \(\mathcal C(x,y)\to\mathcal D(Fx,Fy)\) sending a morphism \(f:x\to y\) in \(\mathcal C\) to a morphism \(Ff:Fx\to Fy\) in \(\mathcal D\);

satisfying the following axioms:

  • \(F\) preserves identities: for each object \(x\in\mathcal C\),

$$F(\operatorname{id}_x)=\operatorname{id}_{Fx};$$

  • \(F\) preserves composites: for all morphisms \(f:x\to y\) and \(g:y\to z\) in \(\mathcal C\),

$$F(g\circ f)=Fg\circ Ff.$$

1.13.html:
Example 1.13. We have the following examples of functors.

  • The forgetful functors \(U:\mathcal{Set}_{\bullet}\to\mathcal{Set}\), \(U:\mathcal{Vect}_k\to\mathcal{Set}\) and \(U:\mathcal{Top}\to\mathcal{Set}\) sending a pointed set, a \(k\)-vector space, or a topological space to its underlying set.
  • The functor \((-)_+:\mathcal{Set}\to\mathcal{Set}_{\bullet}\) which freely adjoins a basepoint to a set \(S\), namely \(S_+:=(S\amalg\{*\},*)\).
  • The functor \(\bigoplus_{(-)}k:\mathcal{Set}\to\mathcal{Vect}_k\) which sends a set \(S\) to the \(k\)-vector space with basis \(S\), namely \(\bigoplus_S k\).
  • The discrete topology functor \(D:\mathcal{Set}\to\mathcal{Top}\) equipping a set \(S\) with the discrete topology, namely \((S,\mathcal P(S))\), where \(\mathcal P(S)\) is the set of subsets of \(S\).
  • The indiscrete topology functor \(I:\mathcal{Set}\to\mathcal{Top}\) equipping a set \(S\) with the indiscrete topology, namely \((S,\{\emptyset,S\})\).

1.14.html:
Proposition 1.14. Let \(F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) be a functor between strict categories. Then \(F\) preserves isomorphisms, i.e., if \(f\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal C\), then \(Ff\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal D\).

Proof. Exercise. \(\square\)

1.15.html:
Construction 1.15. There is a strict category \(\mathcal{Cat}_s\) with

  • object set \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{Cat}_s)\) consisting of the small strict categories;
  • for all objects \(\mathcal C,\mathcal D\in\mathcal{Cat}_s\), hom set \(\mathcal{Cat}_s(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)\) consisting of the functors \(\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\);
  • for each object \(\mathcal C\in\mathcal{Cat}_s\), identity functor \(\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal C}:\mathcal C\to\mathcal C\) acting as the identity on objects and on morphisms;
  • for all morphisms \(F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) and \(G:\mathcal D\to\mathcal E\) in \(\mathcal{Cat}_s\), composite functor \(GF:\mathcal C\to\mathcal E\) sending
    • an object \(x\in\mathcal C\) to the object \(G(F(x))\in\mathcal E\);
    • a morphism \(f:x\to y\) in \(\mathcal C\) to the morphism \(G(F(f)):G(F(x))\to G(F(y))\) in \(\mathcal E\).

This is a well-defined strict category (Exercise).

Similarly, there is a huge strict category \(\mathcal{CAT}_s\) of (large) strict categories and functors.

1.16.html: Remark 1.16. The strict category \(\mathcal{Cat}_s\) of small strict categories and functors defines an object of \(\mathcal{CAT}_s\). As for the other examples, the strict category \(\mathcal{Cat}_s\) is locally small, but not small.

1.17.html:
Construction 1.17. Given a strict category \(\mathcal C\), there is a strict category \(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\), called the opposite strict category of \(\mathcal C\), with

  • object set \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)\);
  • for all objects \(x,y\in\mathcal C\), hom set

$$\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}(x,y):=\mathcal C(y,x);$$

given a morphism \(f:y\to x\) in \(\mathcal C\), we write \(f^{\mathrm{op}}:x\to y\) for the corresponding morphism in \(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\);

  • for each object \(x\in\mathcal C\), identity morphism \((\operatorname{id}_x)^{\mathrm{op}}\);
  • for all morphisms \(f^{\mathrm{op}}:x\to y\) and \(g^{\mathrm{op}}:y\to z\) in \(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\), composite morphism

$$g^{\mathrm{op}}\circ f^{\mathrm{op}}:=(f\circ g)^{\mathrm{op}}:x\to z.$$

This is a well-defined strict category (Exercise).

1.18.html:
Remark 1.18. A contravariant functor from \(\mathcal C\) to \(\mathcal D\) is a functor \(F:\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal D\). It consists of

  • a function \(\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)\to\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal D)\) sending an object \(x\in\mathcal C\) to an object \(Fx\in\mathcal D\);
  • for all objects \(x,y\in\mathcal C\), a function \(\mathcal C(x,y)\to\mathcal D(Fy,Fx)\) sending a morphism \(f:x\to y\) in \(\mathcal C\) to a morphism \(Ff:Fy\to Fx\) in \(\mathcal D\);

satisfying the following axioms:

  • \(F\) preserves identities;
  • \(F\) preserves compositions: for all morphisms \(f:x\to y\) and \(g:y\to z\) in \(\mathcal C\),

$$F(g\circ f)=Ff\circ Fg.$$

1.19.html:
Construction 1.19. Let \(\mathcal C\) be a locally small strict category and \(c\in\mathcal C\) be an object. There is a functor

$$\mathcal C(-,c):\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal{Set},$$

called the representable functor at \(c\), sending:

  • an object \(x\in\mathcal C\) to the (small) set of morphisms \(\mathcal C(x,c)\);
  • a morphism \(f:x\to y\) in \(\mathcal C\) to the function

$$f^*:\mathcal C(y,c)\to\mathcal C(x,c),\quad(g:y\to c)\mapsto(gf:x\to c).$$

This is a well-defined functor (Exercise).

1.20.html:
Definition 1.20. Given functors \(F,G:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) between strict categories, a natural transformation \(\alpha:F\Rightarrow G\) consists of:

  • for each object \(x\in\mathcal C\), a morphism \(\alpha_x:Fx\to Gx\) in \(\mathcal D\), called the component of \(\alpha\) at \(x\);

satisfying the following axiom:

  • \(\alpha\) is natural: for each morphism \(f:x\to y\) in \(\mathcal C\), the following square commutes

i.e., \(Gf\circ\alpha_x=\alpha_y\circ Ff\).

1.21.html:
Construction 1.21. Let \(\mathcal C\) be a locally small strict category and \(f:c\to d\) be a morphism in \(\mathcal C\). There is a natural transformation

$$\mathcal C(-,f):\mathcal C(-,c)\Rightarrow\mathcal C(-,d)$$

whose component at an object \(x\in\mathcal C\) is the function

$$f_*:\mathcal C(x,c)\to\mathcal C(x,d),\quad(g:x\to c)\mapsto(fg:x\to d).$$

This is well-defined (Exercise).

1.22.html:
Definition 1.22. Given functors \(F,G:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) between strict categories, a natural transformation \(\alpha:F\Rightarrow G\) is a natural isomorphism if, for each object \(x\in\mathcal C\), its component \(\alpha_x:Fx\to Gx\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal D\).

We sometimes say that, for all objects \(x\in\mathcal C\), there is an isomorphism \(Fx\cong Gx\) which is natural in \(x\).

1.23.html:
Construction 1.23. Given strict categories \(\mathcal C\) and \(\mathcal D\), there is a strict category \(\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)\), called the functor strict category, with

  • object set \(\operatorname{Ob}(\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)):=\mathcal{CAT}_s(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)\) consisting of the functors \(\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\);
  • for all objects \(F,G\in\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)\), hom set \(\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)(F,G)\) consisting of the natural transformations \(F\Rightarrow G\);
  • for each object \(F\in\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)\), identity natural transformation \(\operatorname{id}_F:F\Rightarrow F\) having component at an object \(c\in\mathcal C\) given by

$$(\operatorname{id}_F)_c:=\operatorname{id}_{Fc}:Fc\to Fc;$$

  • for all morphisms \(\alpha:F\to G\) and \(\beta:G\to H\) in \(\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)\), composite natural transformation \(\beta\circ\alpha:F\Rightarrow H\) having component at an object \(c\in\mathcal C\) given by the composite

$$(\beta\circ\alpha)_c:=\beta_c\circ\alpha_c:Fc\to Hc.$$

This is a well-defined strict category (Exercise).

1.24.html:
Proposition 1.24. Given strict categories \(\mathcal C\) and \(\mathcal D\), a natural transformation is an isomorphism in \(\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal D)\) if and only if it is a natural isomorphism.

Proof. Exercise. \(\square\)

1.25.html: Construction 1.25. The terminal strict category is the strict category \([0]\) with a single object \(*\) and a single morphism \(\operatorname{id}_*\).

1.26.html:
Proposition 1.26. Given a strict category \(\mathcal C\), there is an isomorphism of strict categories

$$\operatorname{Fun}([0],\mathcal C)\cong\mathcal C$$

which is natural in \(\mathcal C\).

Proof. Exercise. \(\square\)

1.27.html: Remark 1.27. As a consequence of this result, we have that an object \(c\in\mathcal C\) corresponds to a unique functor \(c:[0]\to\mathcal C\), which we also call \(c\).

1.28.html:
Construction 1.28. Given a functor \(F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) between strict categories and a strict category \(\mathcal E\), there is a functor

$$F^*:\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal D,\mathcal E)\to\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathcal E),$$

called the precomposition functor with \(F\), sending

  • a functor \(G:\mathcal D\to\mathcal E\) to the composite \(GF:\mathcal C\to\mathcal E\);
  • a natural transformation \(\alpha:G\Rightarrow H\) between functors \(G,H:\mathcal D\to\mathcal E\) to the natural transformation \(\alpha F:GF\Rightarrow HF\) whose component at an object \(x\in\mathcal C\) is the morphism in \(\mathcal E\)

$$\alpha_{Fx}:G(Fx)\to H(Fx).$$

There is also a functor

$$F_*:\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal E,\mathcal C)\to\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal E,\mathcal D),$$

called the postcomposition functor with \(F\), sending

  • a functor \(G:\mathcal E\to\mathcal C\) to the composite \(FG:\mathcal E\to\mathcal D\);
  • a natural transformation \(\alpha:G\Rightarrow H\) between functors \(G,H:\mathcal E\to\mathcal C\) to the natural transformation \(F\alpha:FG\Rightarrow FH\) whose component at an object \(x\in\mathcal E\) is the morphism in \(\mathcal D\)

$$F(\alpha_x):F(Gx)\to F(Hx).$$

These are well-defined functors (Exercise).

2.1.html:
Theorem 2.1 (Yoneda lemma). Let \(\mathcal C\) be a locally small strict category. For all objects \(c\in\mathcal C\) and functors \(F:\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal{Set}\), there is a bijection of sets

$$\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{Set})(\mathcal C(-,c),F)\cong Fc$$

which is natural in both \(c\) and \(F\).

Proof. Evaluation at the identity morphism defines a function

$$\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{Set})(\mathcal C(-,c),F)\to Fc,\quad(\alpha:\mathcal C(-,c)\Rightarrow F)\mapsto\alpha_c(\operatorname{id}_c),$$

where \(\alpha_c:\mathcal C(c,c)\to Fc\) is the function given by the component of \(\alpha\) at \(c\).

Next, consider the function

$$Fc\to\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{Set})(\mathcal C(-,c),F),\quad u\mapsto\alpha_u$$

sending an element \(u\in Fc\) to \(\alpha_u:\mathcal C(-,c)\Rightarrow F\) with component at an object \(x\in\mathcal C\) given by the function

$$(\alpha_u)_x:\mathcal C(x,c)\to Fx,\quad(f:x\to c)\mapsto Ff(u),$$

where \(Ff:Fc\to Fx\) is the function given by the image of \(f\) under \(F\). This is a well-defined natural transformation (Exercise).

These functions are mutually inverse and natural in \(c\) and \(F\) (Exercise). \(\square\)

2.2.html:
Construction 2.2. Let \(\mathcal C\) be a locally small strict category. There is a functor

$$\mathsf y_{\mathcal C}:\mathcal C\to\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{Set})$$

called the Yoneda functor, sending

  • an object \(c\in\mathcal C\) to the representable functor \(\mathcal C(-,c):\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal{Set}\);
  • a morphism \(f:c\to d\) in \(\mathcal C\) to the natural transformation \(\mathcal C(-,f):\mathcal C(-,c)\Rightarrow\mathcal C(-,d)\).

This is well-defined (Exercise).

2.3.html:
Definition 2.3. A functor \(F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) between strict categories is fully faithful if, for all objects \(x,y\in\mathcal C\), the induced function

$$\mathcal C(x,y)\to\mathcal D(Fx,Fy)$$

is a bijection of sets.

2.4.html:
Corollary 2.4. Let \(\mathcal C\) be a locally small strict category. The Yoneda functor

$$\mathsf y_{\mathcal C}:\mathcal C\to\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{Set})$$

is fully faithful.

Proof. Exercise. \(\square\)

2.5.html:
Proposition 2.5. Let \(F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) be a fully faithful functor. Then \(F\) reflects isomorphisms, i.e., if \(f\) is a morphism in \(\mathcal C\) such that \(Ff\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal D\), then \(f\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal C\).

Moreover, two objects \(x,y\in\mathcal C\) are isomorphic if and only if their images \(Fx,Fy\in\mathcal D\) are isomorphic.

Proof. Exercise. \(\square\)

2.6.html:
Corollary 2.6. Let \(\mathcal C\) be a locally small strict category. The following are equivalent for a morphism \(f:c\to d\) in \(\mathcal C\).

(i) The morphism \(f\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal C\).

(ii) For all objects \(x\in\mathcal C\), the induced function

$$f_*:\mathcal C(x,c)\to\mathcal C(x,d)$$

is a bijection of sets.

(iii) For all objects \(x\in\mathcal C\), the induced function

$$f^*:\mathcal C(d,x)\to\mathcal C(c,x)$$

is a bijection of sets.

Proof. Since the Yoneda functor \(\mathsf y_{\mathcal C}:\mathcal C\to\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{Set})\) is fully faithful, it preserves and reflects isomorphisms. Hence the morphism \(f:c\to d\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal C\) if and only if the natural transformation \(\mathcal C(-,f):\mathcal C(-,c)\Rightarrow\mathcal C(-,d)\) is an isomorphism in \(\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{Set})\). By Proposition 1.24, this holds if and only if it is a natural isomorphism, i.e., for every object \(x\in\mathcal C\), the induced morphism

$$f_*:\mathcal C(x,c)\to\mathcal C(x,d)$$

is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal{Set}\). This proves that (i) and (ii) are equivalent.

Next, observe that \(f\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal C\) if and only if \(f^{\mathrm{op}}:d\to c\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\) (Exercise). Then the equivalence between (i) and (ii) for \(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\) implies that \(f^{\mathrm{op}}\) is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\) if and only if, for every object \(x\in\mathcal C\), the induced morphism

$$f^{\mathrm{op}}_*=f^*:\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}(x,d)=\mathcal C(d,x)\to\mathcal C(c,x)=\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}(x,c)$$

is an isomorphism in \(\mathcal{Set}\). This proves that (i) and (iii) are equivalent. \(\square\)

2.7.html:
Corollary 2.7. Let \(\mathcal C\) be a locally small strict category. Two objects \(x,y\in\mathcal C\) are isomorphic if and only if their representable functors \(\mathcal C(-,x)\) and \(\mathcal C(-,y)\) are naturally isomorphic.

Proof. This follows from the preceding proposition applied to the fully faithful Yoneda functor, together with Proposition 1.24. \(\square\)

3.1.html:
Definition 3.1. Given strict categories \(\mathcal C\) and \(\mathcal D\), an adjunction between \(\mathcal C\) and \(\mathcal D\) consists of:

  • a functor \(L:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\), called the left adjoint;
  • a functor \(R:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C\), called the right adjoint;
  • a natural transformation \(\eta:\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal C}\Rightarrow RL\), called the unit;
  • a natural transformation \(\varepsilon:LR\Rightarrow\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal D}\), called the counit;

such that, for all objects \(x\in\mathcal C\) and \(y\in\mathcal D\), the following triangles commute in \(\mathcal D\) and \(\mathcal C\), respectively:

We write \(L:\mathcal C\rightleftarrows\mathcal D:R\) or \(L\dashv R\) for such an adjunction.

3.2.html:
Example 3.2. We have the following examples of adjunctions between strict categories.

  • The free-forgetful adjunctions

$$(-)_+:\mathcal{Set}\rightleftarrows\mathcal{Set}_{\bullet}:U\quad\text{and}\quad\bigoplus_{(-)}k:\mathcal{Set}\rightleftarrows\mathcal{Vect}_k:U.$$

  • The discrete-forgetful and forgetful-indiscrete adjunctions

$$D:\mathcal{Set}\rightleftarrows\mathcal{Top}:U\quad\text{and}\quad U:\mathcal{Top}\rightleftarrows\mathcal{Set}:I.$$

See Example 1.13 for the definition of the functors involved.

3.3.html:
Theorem 3.3 (Adjunctions representably). Given functors \(L:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) and \(R:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C\) between strict categories, there is a unit and a counit making the pair \((L,R)\) into an adjunction \(L\dashv R\) if and only if, for all objects \(x\in\mathcal C\) and \(y\in\mathcal D\), there is a bijection

$$\mathcal D(Lx,y)\cong\mathcal C(x,Ry)$$

which is natural in \(x\) and \(y\).

Proof. Given an adjunction \(L\dashv R\), the unit \(\eta:\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal C}\Rightarrow RL\) induces a function

$$\mathcal D(Lx,y)\xrightarrow{R}\mathcal C(RLx,Ry)\xrightarrow{(\eta_x)^*}\mathcal C(x,Ry),\quad(g:Lx\to y)\mapsto R(g)\circ\eta_x,$$

and the counit \(\varepsilon:LR\Rightarrow\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal D}\) induces a function

$$\mathcal C(x,Ry)\xrightarrow{L}\mathcal D(Lx,LRy)\xrightarrow{(\varepsilon_y)_*}\mathcal D(Lx,y),\quad(f:x\to Ry)\mapsto\varepsilon_y\circ L(f).$$

These are mutually inverse and natural in \(x\) and \(y\) (Exercise).

Conversely, suppose that, for all objects \(x\in\mathcal C\) and \(y\in\mathcal D\), we are given natural bijections

$$\varphi_{x,y}:\mathcal D(Lx,y)\cong\mathcal C(x,Ry).$$

Define \(\eta:\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal C}\Rightarrow RL\) whose component at an object \(x\in\mathcal C\) is given by

$$\eta_x:=\varphi_{x,Lx}(\operatorname{id}_{Lx}):x\to RLx.$$

Define \(\varepsilon:LR\Rightarrow\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal D}\) whose component at an object \(y\in\mathcal D\) is given by the morphism

$$\varepsilon_y:=\varphi^{-1}_{Ry,y}(\operatorname{id}_{Ry}):LRy\to y.$$

These are well-defined natural transformations satisfying the triangle identities (Exercise).

This proves that \(L\dashv R\) is an adjunction. \(\square\)

3.4.html: Definition 3.4. A functor \(F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) between strict categories is an equivalence if there is a functor \(G:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C\) and natural isomorphisms \(\eta:\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal C}\overset{\cong}{\Longrightarrow}GF\) and \(\varepsilon:FG\overset{\cong}{\Longrightarrow}\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal D}\).

3.5.html:
Example 3.5. The following classes of functors give special cases of equivalences.

  • Any isomorphism in \(\mathcal{CAT}_s\) is an equivalence of strict categories.
  • Given an adjunction \(L\dashv R\) such that the unit and the counit are natural isomorphisms, then both \(L\) and \(R\) are equivalences of strict categories; we refer to this as an adjoint equivalence.

Fact: every equivalence of strict categories can be promoted to an adjoint equivalence; see [Rie16, Corollary 4.3.6]. We won’t use this fact in this course.

3.6.html: Definition 3.6. A functor \(F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) between strict categories is essentially surjective if, for all objects \(d\in\mathcal D\), there is an object \(c\in\mathcal C\) and an isomorphism \(\varphi:Fc\overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow}d\) in \(\mathcal D\).

3.7.html:
Theorem 3.7 (Fundamental Theorem). A functor \(F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) between strict categories is an equivalence if and only if it is essentially surjective on objects and fully faithful.

Proof. Next time. \(\square\)

3.8.html: Construction 3.8. The walking isomorphism is the strict category \(\mathcal I:=\{0\cong1\}\) with two objects \(0\) and \(1\), whose only morphisms are the identities and mutually inverse isomorphisms \(f:0\to1\) and \(f^{-1}:1\to0\). Observe that the hom sets of \(\mathcal I\) are all singletons.

3.9.html:
Proposition 3.9. The functor \(0:[0]\to\mathcal I\) is an equivalence of strict categories.

Proof. It is surjective on objects up to isomorphisms, since \(0\cong0\) in \(\mathcal I\), and it is fully faithful since, for the unique object \(*\in[0]\), we have a bijection

$$[0](*,*)=\{\operatorname{id}_*\}\overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow}\{\operatorname{id}_0\}=\mathcal I(0,0).\quad\square$$

intro.what.html:
Informally, an \(\infty\)-category consists of

  • objects \(x,y,\ldots\);
  • morphisms \(f:x\to y\) between objects;
  • 2-morphisms

between parallel morphisms

  • 3-morphisms between parallel 2-morphisms;
  • and so on;

such that all \(k\)-morphisms for \(k\geq2\) are invertible, in a suitably weak sense. Composition is associative and unital up to higher invertible morphisms, which themselves satisfy compatibility conditions in all higher dimensions.

intro.paths.html:
A motivating example comes from topology. Given a topological space \(X\), consider the \(\infty\)-category whose:

  • objects are points of \(X\);
  • morphisms are paths between points in \(X\);

  • 2-morphisms are homotopies between paths, fixing the endpoints;

  • 3-morphisms are homotopies between homotopies, fixing the boundaries;
  • and so on.

Composition is given by concatenating paths and homotopies. Concatenation of paths is associative and unital up to homotopy: different ways of composing the same paths need not give exactly the same parametrised path, but they can be continuously deformed into one another. Moreover, reversing a path gives an inverse up to homotopy. Thus, in this example, even the morphisms are invertible in the appropriate sense. Such a structure is called an \(\infty\)-groupoid.

intro.models.html:
Traditionally, \(\infty\)-categories have been studied through concrete models, such as quasi-categories [Joy08, Lur09] and complete Segal spaces [Rez01, Ras23]. These models make the informal description above precise using constructions within set-theoretic foundations. Encoding \(\infty\)-categories in set-theoretic terms can make them difficult to work with: questions about intrinsic categorical properties may become hard combinatorial problems involving the chosen model.

In this course, we will take an axiomatic approach to \(\infty\)-category theory. Our approach differs from the model-based one described above in the following aspects: the foundations, including the structure identity principle, and the synthetic approach.

intro.hott.html:
Homotopy type theory. The first aspect is a change of foundations. In ordinary set-based mathematics, given a set \(X\) and elements \(x,y\in X\), the expression \(x=y\) is a proposition: it is either true or false, and carries no further structure describing an identification between \(x\) and \(y\).

In homotopy type theory, our basic objects are types. We write \(x:X\) to say that \(x\) is a term, or element, of the type \(X\). Given terms \(x,y:X\), the expression

$$x=y$$

is itself a type, called an identity type. Its terms can be thought of as paths identifying \(x\) and \(y\). Given two such terms \(p,q:x=y\), we can form another identity type

$$p=q,$$

whose terms can be thought of as homotopies between these paths. This process continues indefinitely.

A type therefore already carries higher-dimensional structure: terms, identifications between terms, identifications between identifications, and so on. These identifications behave like paths and higher homotopies in a space, so types naturally behave as \(\infty\)-groupoids. The higher structure is built into our foundations.

intro.sip.html:
The structure identity principle. When studying mathematical structures in classical foundations, one must distinguish between properties that are invariant under isomorphism and those that depend on the chosen presentation. For example, given a group \(G\), the property “\(G\) contains an element of order 2” is invariant under group isomorphism, whereas “the identity element of \(G\) is the number 0” is not. Indeed, the groups \((\{0,1\},+\text{mod }2)\) and \((\{1,-1\},\cdot)\) are isomorphic, but the latter property holds only for the first. Both properties can be expressed in set-theoretic foundations, but only the first describes the abstract group structure.

An inbuild feature of equality, both in set-theoretic foundations and in homotopy type theory, is the indiscernibility principle: if \(x=y\), then any property of \(x\) also holds for \(y\), and any additional structure on \(x\) can be transported to \(y\), and vice-versa.

Homotopy type theory allows for an additional feature that is inconceivable in classical foundations: namely the structure identity principle. It connects equality with the mathematical notion of having the same structure. For example, given groups \(G\) and \(H\), the terms of the identity type \(G=H\) correspond precisely to group isomorphisms from \(G\) to \(H\). Thus, giving an identification of two groups amounts to giving an isomorphism between them. The identity type records not just whether the groups can be identified, but also how they are identified.

Combined with indiscernibility, this implies that every property or construction of groups expressible in this framework is invariant under isomorphism. Invariance under isomorphism is therefore built into the foundations.

intro.synthetic.html:
Synthetic category theory. The second aspect is the synthetic viewpoint itself. Rather than beginning with a concrete construction of an \(\infty\)-category, we will specify axioms describing how \(\infty\)-categories and the relationships between them behave. Our emphasis will therefore shift from the question “What is an \(\infty\)-category?” to “How does the collection of \(\infty\)-categories behave?” This requires a sufficiently rich axiomatic setting, but allows us to develop the theory directly from its structural properties.

To do this, we extend homotopy type theory so that we can also talk about non-invertible morphisms. In this framework, \(\infty\)-categories are basic types, and we retain the core principles of homotopy type theory, such as the structure identity principle.

intro.course.html:
We will begin with a brief introduction to ordinary category theory, which we will call strict category theory throughout these notes. The aim is to become familiar with examples and basic constructions before encountering their \(\infty\)-categorical counterparts. We will then survey the foundations of homotopy type theory, following [Rij25, Uni13]. Next, we will pass to an extension of this type theory, which is inspired from [Riv25] and formulate the axioms of synthetic category theory in this extended type theory. This approach to the foundations differs from the one presented in [CCNW21]. We will then develop category theory in this synthetic setting, following [CCNW21].

We plan to cover adjunctions, localisations, left and cocartesian fibrations, the Yoneda lemma, left and right Kan extensions, and limits and colimits. These names need not be familiar at this stage: the course will introduce them progressively, explaining both their meaning and their role.

strict.motivation.html: In this first part, we introduce or recall various definitions and constructions in ordinary category theory that will later be generalized to the \(\infty\)-setting. Our aim is to build intuition for the kinds of structures and results we will encounter, so that the abstract setting introduced later feels less intimidating. We will also highlight some of the limitations of strict categories and explain why they can be too rigid to do category theory. For instance, working with sets of objects and morphisms encourages us to formulate notions in terms of equality of objects, which can lead to constructions that are not invariant under equivalences of strict categories. Understanding this distinction, and the difficulties it creates, will motivate the synthetic approach to category theory developed later in the course.

equivalences.motivation.html:
3. Adjunctions and equivalences

We now turn to two important concepts in strict category theory, namely adjunctions and equivalences. Adjunctions provide a way to describe universal constructions and organize them into functors. Equivalences express when two strict categories should be thought of as being the “same”.

From a categorical point of view, two isomorphic objects should be interchangeable, even if they are not equal. However, an isomorphism of strict categories requires a bijection between the sets of objects, making it too restrictive for this purpose. Equivalences provide a weakening of the notion of isomorphism between strict categories and capture the intended notion of sameness: they detect objects only up to isomorphism, rather than up to equality.

A fundamental difficulty with the set-theoretic description of strict categories is that equality and isomorphism of objects remain distinct notions. Consequently, properties and constructions can depend on literal equalities between objects and fail to be well-behaved with respect to isomorphisms. We will illustrate this with examples of properties and constructions that are not invariant under replacing objects by isomorphic ones or strict categories by equivalent ones. Further examples will appear in the following sections.

The synthetic approach will address this foundational issue by not allowing a distinction between equality and isomorphism of objects, so that invariance under isomorphism is built into the theory. Similarly, the appropriate notion of isomorphism between synthetic categories will generalize that of an equivalence between strict categories.

3.5.adjoint_upgrade.html: Fact: every equivalence of strict categories can be promoted to an adjoint equivalence; see [Rie16, Corollary 4.3.6]. We won’t use this fact in this course.

intro.higher_morphisms.html:
Informally, an \(\infty\)-category consists of

  • objects \(x,y,\ldots\);
  • morphisms \(f:x\to y\) between objects;
  • 2-morphisms

between parallel morphisms

  • 3-morphisms between parallel 2-morphisms;
  • and so on;

such that all \(k\)-morphisms for \(k\geq2\) are invertible, in a suitably weak sense. Composition is associative and unital up to higher invertible morphisms, which themselves satisfy compatibility conditions in all higher dimensions.

intro.invertibility.html:

  • morphisms \(f:x\to y\) between objects;
  • 2-morphisms

between parallel morphisms

  • 3-morphisms between parallel 2-morphisms;
  • and so on;

such that all \(k\)-morphisms for \(k\geq2\) are invertible, in a suitably weak sense. Composition is associative and unital up to higher invertible morphisms, which themselves satisfy compatibility conditions in all higher dimensions.
